title: Go Signal
teaches: The Go Signal as we trade it, on hourly bars: a leader in an uptrend pulls back to support, the first hourly candle trades under the prior day's close, and buyers push it back above that close by the end of the second hourly candle. The stop sits a few cents under the session low at the time of entry, a third comes off at 3R and 5R, and a turn after the second candle is a pivot, not a Go Signal.

questions.q: On a Go Signal, red to green is measured against which price?
choices: The prior day's close
The candle's open
The low of the flag
The day's VWAP line
questions.why: The prior day's close. Red to green on a Go Signal is measured against the prior day's close. It is not the hourly candle's own open and not a flag low. A candle that closes above its own open is only green.
questions.lesson_line: The line is yesterday's close. Nothing else.

wrong.The candle's open: A candle that merely closes above its own open is green, not a Go Signal. The line is the prior close.
wrong.The low of the flag: The card says it is not measured against a flag low.
wrong.The day's VWAP line: The card names only the prior day's close as the line.

questions.simple: The line is the prior day's close, because the stock first trades under it and then climbs back above it.

questions.q: A Go Signal needs the first hourly candle to trade below the prior day's close.
questions.why: True. A Go Signal needs the first hourly candle to trade below the prior day's close. Early in the session the stock trades under that close. Then buyers push it back above in the first or second hourly candle. A gap up that never trades under the prior close is not a Go Signal.
questions.lesson_line: Under the prior close first, then back over it.
questions.simple: True, because the stock must first trade under the prior close before buyers push it back above.

questions.q: By the end of which hourly candle must the stock be back above the prior close?
choices: The second candle
The first candle only
The fourth candle
The last of the day
questions.why: The second. The reclaim must come by the end of the second hourly candle. So a turn in the first or the second candle counts. A turn after that is a pivot (setup 41), not a Go Signal.
questions.lesson_line: First or second candle. After that it is a pivot.

wrong.The last of the day: A turn that late is a pivot. The Go Signal lives in the first two candles.
wrong.The first candle only: The first or the second candle counts. A turn in the second is still a Go Signal.
wrong.The fourth candle: By the fourth candle it is a pivot, not a Go Signal.

questions.simple: The stock must be back above the prior close by the end of the second hourly candle, or it is a pivot.

reasons: rests on the owner's criteria card (settled, D-145) (+2)

questions.why: False. A gap up that never trades under the prior close is not a Go Signal. The dip under the prior close comes first.

questions.why: 3. We take no new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. An open trade can be held through the report only if it is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Three sessions before a report: no new buy.
questions.simple: We take no new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B22 (+2)

questions.q: A Go Signal is bought with a market order.
questions.why: True. Entries are market orders. The rule covers every entry we take, not only the Go Signal.
questions.lesson_line: Entries are market orders.
questions.simple: Yes, we buy with a market order.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E57 and D41 (+2); the order moment itself (D-003) is not keyed

questions.q: A Go Signal can be bought in the after-hours session.
questions.why: False. No new buys outside regular trading hours, and after-hours is outside them. The card also says regular hours only, and the signal lives in the first two hourly candles by definition. Neither an order type nor good news changes that.
questions.lesson_line: Regular hours only.
questions.simple: False, because we make no new buys outside regular hours and the Go Signal lives in the first two hourly candles.

reasons: rests on our rulebook and card (+2)

questions.q: A red to green turn is common. What is the edge in a Go Signal?
choices: The stock and the level
The hour the turn comes in
The size of the candle
Heavy volume on the reclaim
questions.why: The stock and the level. The card says the turn itself is not the edge. A Go Signal needs the setup around it: a leader that already moved, a tight hourly flag, and a dip into the 20-day line or a marked level.
questions.lesson_line: The turn is common. The stock and the level are the edge.

wrong.The hour the turn comes in: The two-candle window is a gate, but the card says the stock and the level are the edge.
wrong.The size of the candle: The card names the stock and the level as the edge, not the size of one candle.
wrong.Heavy volume on the reclaim: Volume on the reclaim is not what the card calls the edge. The stock and the level are.

questions.simple: The stock and the level, because the turn itself is common and the card calls them the edge.

deeper.trap: A big, fast turn feels like the edge. The card says the turn itself is common. The stock and the level behind it are what count.

reasons: rests on held decisions D-130, D-131, D-132 (+2)

questions.q: A dip under the prior close, then a close back above it by candle two. In our scan, that happens in about a third of liquid sessions.
questions.why: True. In our scan the turn happens in about a third of all liquid sessions. A turn that common is not an edge by itself. The edge is the stock and the level. That means a leader that already moved, a tight hourly flag, and a dip into the 20-day line or a marked level.
questions.lesson_line: A common turn is not an edge by itself.
questions.simple: True, because in our scan this turn shows up in about a third of liquid sessions, so it is not an edge.

reasons: a statistic from our own scan that can be re-measured, not a published figure (+2)
rests on the owner's criteria card (settled, D-145) (+2)

questions.q: Where does the Go Signal stop go?
choices: Just under the session low
Under the 20-day EMA
Under the low of the hourly flag
At the reclaimed level
questions.why: A few cents under the session low at the time of entry, not exactly on it. It does not go under the flag, the 20-day EMA or the reclaimed level.
questions.lesson_line: The low of the day is the line you defend.

wrong.Under the 20-day EMA: The average is context. The stop goes under the low of the session.
wrong.At the reclaimed level: Never raise the stop to the reclaimed level: the level is where the shake-out happens.
wrong.Under the low of the hourly flag: The flag low is not the line. The stop is under the session low at the time of entry.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the low of the session, because that low is the line you defend.

deeper.example: In our scan, META had a session low of 331.66 and the stop went to 331.63, a few cents under it. That stop sat 1.42% from the 336.42 buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop rule, F62 (+2)

questions.q: A stop that is too wide should be raised to the reclaimed level so the trade fits.
questions.why: False. Never raise the stop to the reclaimed level to make it fit. The level is where the shake-out happens, so a stop there gets taken out. If the honest stop is too far, size down or skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Do not tighten the stop to the reclaimed level.
questions.simple: False, because the reclaimed level is where the shake-out happens, so size down or skip instead.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, go.stop_not_raised, and the owner's stop rule (+2)

questions.q: A Go Signal needs the stock above its 50-day SMA.
questions.why: True. The card wants the price above the 50-day SMA. It lists a Go Signal in a downtrend, under the 50-day or 200-day, as a mistake. The 200-day is its own rule: no longs below it, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 50-day and the 200-day.
questions.simple: True, because the card wants the price above the 50-day line and lists a Go Signal under it as a mistake.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, go.above_50 (+2)

questions.q: Tap the level that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A trade still under ___ after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.why: 1R. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. The time stop does not wait for the stop to be hit. It is not set at breakeven, which starts at 2R, or at the first trim, which is 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days under 1R: out.
questions.simple: A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, which frees up the money.

questions.q: A clean turn at 14:00 is still a Go Signal if the candle is strong.
questions.why: False. A turn after the second hourly candle is a pivot, not a Go Signal, however clean the candle.
questions.lesson_line: The clock decides. After the second candle it is a pivot.

questions.q: How does an Oops differ from a Go Signal?
choices: The Oops is a daily bar at the prior low
The Oops uses hourly bars
The Oops uses the prior close
They are the same
questions.answer: The Oops is a daily bar at the prior low
questions.why: The Oops is a daily bar at the prior low. An Oops gaps below the prior day's low and closes back above it; the Go Signal's line is the prior close.
questions.lesson_line: Oops: daily, prior low. Go Signal: hourly, prior close.

wrong.The Oops uses hourly bars: The Oops is read on the daily bar. The Go Signal is read on the first two hourly candles.
wrong.The Oops uses the prior close: The Oops line is the prior day's low. The Go Signal line is the prior day's close.

questions.q: A Go Signal wants a 20-day EMA that is higher than it was 5 sessions ago.
questions.why: True. The card wants a rising 20-day EMA. The test is that it is higher than it was 5 sessions ago.
questions.lesson_line: The 20-day EMA should be rising.

questions.q: Entry 37.18. The session low is 36.15 and the stop sits 3 cents under it. How far below the entry, in percent, to two decimals?
questions.why: 2.85%. The stop sits 3 cents under the 36.15 session low. Measured from the 37.18 entry, that distance is 2.85%. A stop within about 3% fits. Past about 3%, we size down or skip.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent before you size it.
questions.simple: The stop is 3 cents under the 36.15 low, so it sits 2.85 percent below the 37.18 entry.

deeper.example: META: bought at 336.42 with the stop at 331.63, which is 1.42% away. VIAV: bought at 26.43 with the stop at 25.66, which is 2.91% away. Both fit inside about 3%.

questions.q: Prior close 168.84. The reclaim candle closes at 169.79. How far over the prior close, in percent, to one decimal?
questions.why: 0.6%. Measure from the prior close, 168.84, because it is the buy point. The reclaim close of 169.79 is about 0.6% above it. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. At 0.6% the chase rule does not block the buy. Chasing costs size, not risk.
questions.lesson_line: Check the distance from the prior close before you buy.
questions.simple: That is 0.6 percent over the prior close, far under the 4 percent chase limit.

questions.q: Bought at 336.42 with the stop at 331.63. One R is the gap between them. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 350.79. One R is the fill minus the stop, 336.42 minus 331.63. Three R is the fill plus three of those. The hard rule is a third off at 3R. Ideally the first trim comes anywhere from 3R to 6R.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open.
questions.simple: Three R is the fill plus three times the gap between fill and stop, which gives 350.79.

questions.q: Which rule decides this buy?
choices: No new buy 3 sessions before a report
No new buy over 4% above the buy point
Skip a long 10% over its 10-day line
Buy only in regular trading hours
questions.answer: No new buy 3 sessions before a report
questions.why: No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. This stock reports in two sessions, so it is inside the window. The setup is fine, but the calendar decides. A day later the report is closer still.
questions.lesson_line: Report inside 3 sessions: no new buy.

wrong.No new buy over 4% above the buy point: That rule is real, but the story gives no price above the buy point.
wrong.Skip a long 10% over its 10-day line: That rule is real, but the story says nothing about the 10-day line.
wrong.Buy only in regular trading hours: That rule is real, but the story is a first-hour reclaim, inside regular hours.

questions.story: A perfect first-hour reclaim at the 20-day line. The stock reports earnings in two sessions.
questions.simple: The rule is no new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report, and this stock reports in two sessions.

deeper.trap: The 5R line in our rulebook is about holding a trade through a report, and only if it is up 5R. It does not let you open a new buy inside the 3-session window.

reasons: rests on our rulebook and card (+2)

questions.q: Is this a Go Signal?
choices: No; it never went red first
Yes; green all morning
Yes; if the 20-day rises
No; it needs more volume
questions.answer: No; it never went red first
questions.why: No. A gap up that never trades under the prior close is not a Go Signal. The first hourly candle has to trade under the prior close first, and then buyers push it back above. A stock that is green from the open has no turn in it. A rising 20-day or heavier volume does not make one.
questions.lesson_line: No red, no red to green.

wrong.Yes; green all morning: Green is not red to green. There was no red first.
wrong.Yes; if the 20-day rises: A rising 20-day is context. Without a dip under the prior close there is no signal.
wrong.No; it needs more volume: Volume is not a rule for the Go Signal. What is missing is the dip under the prior close.

questions.story: The stock opens 0.8% above the prior close and never trades under it. It grinds green all morning.
questions.simple: No, because the stock never traded under the prior close, so there was no red to green to buy.

reasons: which open counts is held (D-128); the key uses only the settled rule (+2)

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A Go Signal
A daily U&R
A late pivot
A daily Oops
questions.why: A Go Signal. Its undercut and reclaim happen inside the first two hours of one session and are measured against the prior close. A U&R undercuts a prominent prior swing low and closes back above it within 3 sessions on the daily chart. An Oops is a daily bar read at the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: One session, prior close, hourly: a Go Signal.

wrong.A daily U&R: A U&R needs a prominent prior swing low and gives it up to 3 sessions on the daily chart. This is one session, hourly.
wrong.A late pivot: A pivot is a turn after the second hourly candle. Here candle two already closed back above the prior close.
wrong.A daily Oops: An Oops is a daily bar at the prior day's low. This line is the prior close.

questions.story: A leader rests on its 20-day line in a tight hourly flag. In one session the first hourly candle dips under the prior close. The second hourly candle closes back above it.
questions.simple: It is a Go Signal, because the dip and the reclaim happen in one session against the prior close.

deeper.counter: A U&R is a daily setup. The stock undercuts a level and must close back above it within 3 sessions. The Go Signal packs its undercut and reclaim into the first two hours of one session.

questions.q: Sell at the close, or hold?
choices: Hold; it is a warning only
Sell at the close; it failed
Move the stop up to 90.55
Cut half now and hold the rest
questions.answer: Hold; it is a warning only
questions.why: Hold. A day that closes back under the prior close is a warning, not an exit. Those trades averaged -0.47R, but selling them at the close did not improve the average. The stop is still the exit, so you hold while the price stays above 89.39.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the prior close is a warning. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Move the stop up to 90.55: Never raise the stop to the reclaimed level.
wrong.Sell at the close; it failed: Selling at that close did not improve the average. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Cut half now and hold the rest: The plan trims at 3R and 5R, not on a warning. The stop is the exit.

questions.story: You bought a first-candle reclaim at 90.98 with the stop at 89.39. At 15:50 the stock is 90.41, under the prior close 90.55, above your stop.
questions.simple: Hold, because a close under the prior close is only a warning and your stop is still the exit.

deeper.counter: Here, selling at 90.41 would have lost less than the 89.39 stop did. That is one trade. The card looks at the average of all such trades, which was -0.47R, and selling at the close did not improve it. Judge the rule on the average, not on the one that stings.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, go.close_under_pc_warning, and the old template says otherwise (+2)
a statistic from our own scan (+2)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Sell it all and take the loss
Set the stop at 118.83, hold
Keep the 123.39 stop, wait
Buy more at the lower price
questions.answer: Sell it all and take the loss
questions.why: Get out. A gap through the stop hands the stop to the first 30-minute low. But if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here 1R is 3.42. The stock is at 119.40 and the low is 118.83, both more than 2R under your 126.81 buy.
questions.lesson_line: First 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, out.

wrong.Set the stop at 118.83, hold: The first 30-minute low is the new stop, but only up to a ceiling. Past 2R, you are out.
wrong.Keep the 123.39 stop, wait: The stock is already through it. The gap rule hands the stop to the first 30 minutes.
wrong.Buy more at the lower price: The full size goes in at one price with one stop. A second buy breaks that.

questions.story: You bought at 126.81 with the stop at 123.39, so 1R is 3.42. The next morning gaps down to 121.00. The first 30-minute low is 118.83, and after 30 minutes the stock sits at 119.40.
questions.simple: Get out, because a gap through the stop hands it to the first 30-minute low unless that loss is past 2R.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the gap rule as a free pass. The first 30-minute low becomes the new stop only while the loss stays within 2R. Here 1R is 3.42. The low of 118.83 is more than twice that under 126.81, so the answer is out, whatever the stock does next.

reasons: a computed key: the loss at the 30-minute low against 2R (+2)
rests on the owner's gap rule, B20 (+2)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take a third off at the open
Wait for 25.89 on the way down
Hold it all and trail it up
Sell it all at the open now
questions.answer: Take a third off at the open
questions.why: Take the first third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open. It opens at 26.40, past the 3R level of 25.89, so the first third comes off at once. The next third waits for 5R, and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: Gap past a trim level: take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for 25.89 on the way down: A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open, not on a later dip.
wrong.Hold it all and trail it up: The trail is for the last third, after the trims.
wrong.Sell it all at the open now: The plan is a third at 3R, a third at 5R, then the trail.

questions.story: You bought at 24.48 with the stop at 24.01. Your 3R level is 25.89. The next morning the stock opens at 26.40.
questions.simple: Take a third off at the open, because a stock that opens past a trim level gets that trim at the open.

reasons: rests on the owner's trim rules, F63 and B19 (+2)

questions.q: What trails the last third of a Go Signal in a fast mover?
choices: A close under the 10-day line
A close under the 200-day line
A new 5-day closing low
The low of the entry day
questions.why: A close under the 10-day average. The last third trails the 10-day for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. You sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Fast stock, 10-day. Steady stock, 21-day.

wrong.A close under the 200-day line: That is not our trail. We trail the 10-day for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones.
wrong.A new 5-day closing low: A short-term low is not our trail. We use the 10-day or the 21-day.
wrong.The low of the entry day: That is the first stop, and it only moves up. The last third trails an average instead.

questions.simple: A fast mover is trailed with the 10-day average, and you sell on a close below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's trail rule, E52 (+2)

questions.q: What now?
choices: Sell; under 1R at 10 sessions
Hold; the stop has not been hit
Add to it while it is quiet
Move the stop to breakeven
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, which frees the money.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions, under 1R: out.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not been hit: The stop is not the only exit. A trade still under 1R after 10 sessions is sold.
wrong.Add to it while it is quiet: We do not add. The money is better used on a new setup.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R, not at 0.4R.

questions.story: Ten sessions after the buy, the stock sits at 0.4R. The stop has not been hit and no trim has come off.

questions.q: Skip the buy if the reclaim candle closes more than 4% above the prior close.
questions.why: True. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and for a Go Signal the buy point is the prior close. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the prior close and I am done.
questions.simple: True, because we never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and here that point is the prior close.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, C28 (+2)

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 0.25%. Buy 336.42, stop 331.63. How many shares does the stop allow?
questions.why: 52 shares. Risk is 0.25% of 100,000. Divide it by the distance from the 336.42 buy to the 331.63 stop, then round down to 52. The size is the smaller of the risk size and the position cap. The cap is 40% of the account, and 52 shares are well under it.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Not the other way round.
questions.simple: Divide the risk, 0.25 percent of 100,000, by the distance from buy to stop, then round down to 52 shares.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Size down or skip; never raise the stop
Raise the stop to the reclaimed level
Buy full size anyway
Use the 20-day EMA as the stop
questions.answer: Size down or skip; never raise the stop
questions.why: Size down or skip. If the stop is more than about 3% away, size down or skip; never raise it to the reclaimed level.
questions.lesson_line: Wide stop: fewer shares, or no trade.

wrong.Raise the stop to the reclaimed level: Never raise the stop to the reclaimed level. That is where the shake-out happens.
wrong.Buy full size anyway: The size comes from the stop. A wide stop means fewer shares or no trade.
wrong.Use the 20-day EMA as the stop: The stop is under the session low. An average is not the stop.

questions.story: A clean Go Signal sets up. The honest stop, a few cents under the session low, is 5.5% below the buy.

questions.q: The turn is valid. What do you do?
choices: Size down from the stop
Buy full size; ignore the stop width
Tighten the stop to fit it
Buy the open, skip the wait
questions.why: Size down from the stop. The turn is valid, and the stop under the first candle's low is 4.96% from the entry. We prefer 1 to 3%, and up to 5% is acceptable. So we take it with fewer shares. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A giant first candle widens the stop. Size follows the stop.

wrong.Tighten the stop to fit it: Never move the stop up to make a trade fit. The honest stop marks the real low.
wrong.Buy the open, skip the wait: The open is before the turn. Buying it is the blind open buy.
wrong.Buy full size; ignore the stop width: Full size on a stop 4.96% away risks more than planned. The size comes from the stop.

questions.story: After a 2.8% gap down the first candle runs from 315.73 to 329.02. The stop under its low is 4.96% from the entry.
questions.simple: Size down from the stop. It is 4.96% away, inside the 5% we accept, so it only means fewer shares.

reasons: how wide a stop may be is held (D-005) (+2)

questions.q: Take it?
choices: Yes; a new trade, its own stop
No; it failed on Monday
Yes; with a wider stop
No; one try a week, no more
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade, its own stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade with its own stop. After a stop-out you buy again only if the setup triggers again, and then it is a new trade with every rule. This is the second try this week and this month. That is inside the limit of 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock.
questions.lesson_line: A new trigger is a new trade. Count the tries.

wrong.No; it failed on Monday: A new trigger is a new trade. The limit is 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock.
wrong.Yes; with a wider stop: The stop sits a few cents under the session low. A wider one to get back in is not the rule.
wrong.No; one try a week, no more: The limit is 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. Two tries is well inside it.

questions.story: A Go Signal in this stock failed on Monday, the only try this month. On Wednesday it sets up and turns again, a fresh trigger.
questions.simple: Yes, because a fresh trigger is a new trade with its own stop, and a second try is inside the limit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B21 and E56 (+2)

questions.q: Can you take it?
choices: Yes; only the top grade passes
Yes, but only at half size
No; only a Green reading trades
No; Orange means mostly cash
questions.answer: Yes; only the top grade passes
questions.why: Yes. In an Orange market reading we take only A+ setups, and this one grades A plus. Yellow is smaller and fewer, which is a different reading.
questions.lesson_line: Orange means A plus only. An A plus still goes.

wrong.No; Orange means mostly cash: Orange allows A+ setups, so this one can go.
wrong.Yes, but only at half size: Smaller and fewer is the Yellow reading. In Orange the rule is A+ only.

questions.story: The market reading is Orange. A Go Signal sets up cleanly, and you grade it A plus.
questions.simple: Yes, because an Orange market reading allows only A plus setups and this one grades A plus.

reasons: rests on our rulebook and card (+2)

questions.q: Heavy volume on the reclaim is a hard rule for the Go Signal.
questions.why: False. Volume is not a rule. More volume on the reclaim than on the flag's first hours is a plus for grading, not a gate. Gil Morales says the same of his U&R: volume is generally not a factor.
questions.lesson_line: Volume grades the signal. It does not gate it.
questions.simple: False, because volume is not a rule and more of it on the reclaim is only a plus when grading.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, go.volume (D-006) (+2)

questions.q: Take it?
choices: Pass; no longs under the 200-day
Take it; the 20-day is rising
Take it, but only at half size
Pass; it came too late in the day
questions.why: Pass. The Go Signal needs the price above the 200-day SMA, and our rule is no longs below it. It is a hard rule, so a rising 20-day or a smaller size does not lift it.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day is a hard line. Under it, no Go Signal.

wrong.Take it; the 20-day is rising: A rising 20-day is one gate. The 200-day is another, and it is a hard rule.
wrong.Take it, but only at half size: Half size does not lift a hard rule.
wrong.Pass; it came too late in the day: The story calls it a first-hour reclaim, so the timing is fine. The 200-day is the problem.

questions.story: A textbook first-hour reclaim at a rising 20-day EMA. The stock is under its 200-day SMA.
questions.simple: Pass, because we take no longs under the 200-day line and this stock is under it.

reasons: rests on the owner's hard 200-day rule, B26 (+2)

questions.q: Take it?
choices: Pass; it is under the 50-day
Take it; the turn looks clean
Take it; the 200-day still holds
Pass; the 200-day rule blocks it
questions.why: Pass. The card wants the price above the 50-day, and this stock is under it. The card also lists a Go Signal taken in a downtrend, under the 50-day or 200-day, as a mistake. The Go Signal needs the setup around the turn, so a clean turn alone does not change the answer.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 50-day is a downtrend. Pass.

wrong.Take it; the turn looks clean: A clean turn under the 50-day is a listed mistake.
wrong.Take it; the 200-day still holds: The 200-day is one line. The card also wants the price above the 50-day.
wrong.Pass; the 200-day rule blocks it: The stock is above its 200-day, so that rule passes. The 50-day is the problem.

questions.story: A first-hour reclaim of the prior close in a stock under its 50-day but above its 200-day.
questions.simple: Pass, because the card wants the price above the 50-day and this stock is under it.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, go.above_50 (+2)

questions.q: What is wrong with that?
choices: There is no signal to buy yet
Nothing; early entries do better
Half size is the safe way in
A wider stop would make it fine
questions.answer: There is no signal to buy yet
questions.why: There is no signal yet. At 9:35 the stock is still under the prior close, so the turn has not happened. Buying the open before the turn is the blind open buy, and it gets stopped at the low. Wait for the stock to get back above the prior close.
questions.lesson_line: Do not buy the red. Wait for the green.

wrong.Nothing; early entries do better: Buying the open before the turn gets stopped at the low. The turn is the signal.
wrong.Half size is the safe way in: Half size does not fix a buy before the turn.
wrong.A wider stop would make it fine: A wider stop does not fix the timing.

questions.story: At 9:35 the stock is red, 1% under the prior close. You buy now to get ahead of the turn.
questions.simple: The stock has not turned yet, so there is nothing to buy until it is back above the prior close.

reasons: rests on the owner's criteria card, go.entry mistake (+2)

questions.q: Bought at 26.43, stop 25.66. One R is the gap between them. The stock trades to 28.74. How many R is that?
questions.why: 3R. One R is the fill minus the stop, 26.43 minus 25.66. The move from 26.43 to 28.74 is exactly three of those. The hard rule takes a third off at 3R. VIAV got there in 3 days.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R. Three R is the first trim.
questions.simple: The stock is up three times the gap between fill and stop, so the trade is at 3R.

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A pivot, not a Go Signal
A Go Signal, a little late
An Oops at the prior low
A Remount of the prior close
questions.answer: A pivot, not a Go Signal
questions.why: A pivot, not a Go Signal. AXON closed back above the prior close, 359.35, on the third hourly candle, after the two-candle window. The reclaim has to come by the end of the second candle. It is a 30-minute pivot, bought over the pivot candle's high, not at a candle close.
questions.lesson_line: A third-candle turn is a pivot.

wrong.A Go Signal, a little late: There is no late version. After the second candle it is a pivot.
wrong.An Oops at the prior low: An Oops is a daily bar at the prior low.
wrong.A Remount of the prior close: Nothing here is a long-lost line retaken. The prior close was reclaimed, just too late.

questions.story: The close back above the prior close, 359.35, comes on the third hourly candle at 361.39. Everything else passes.
questions.simple: It is a pivot, because the reclaim came on the third candle, after the two-candle window.

deeper.example: AXON, 2024-09-11: the third hourly candle closed at 361.39, above the prior close of 359.35. Every other gate passed, but the clock failed. A pivot is its own setup, bought over the pivot candle's high.

questions.q: Is this a Go Signal?
choices: No; a bare turn with no flag
Yes; it turned inside the window
Yes; news days give strong turns
No; only candle one counts
questions.answer: No; a bare turn with no flag
questions.why: No. A red to green inside a wild post-earnings range, with no tight flag to buy against, is a bare red to green. The clock is only one gate. The card also needs the setup around the turn. That is a leader that already moved, a tight hourly flag, and a dip into the 20-day line or a marked level. SNOW had this shape.
questions.lesson_line: No flag, no Go Signal. Just a common turn.

wrong.Yes; it turned inside the window: The clock is only one gate. The turn also needs the setup around it.
wrong.Yes; news days give strong turns: A wild range after earnings leaves no tight flag to defend.
wrong.No; only candle one counts: The first or the second candle counts. Here the turn is on time; the missing flag is the problem.

questions.story: The stock swings wildly after earnings, with no tight flag. The first candle dips under the prior close and the next closes above it.
questions.simple: No, because the turn came on time but a wild range with no tight flag leaves nothing to buy against.

deeper.trap: The trap is the clock. The turn came on time, in candle two, so it feels like a Go Signal. But the card wants the setup around it. That is a leader that already moved, a tight hourly flag, and a dip into the 20-day line or a marked level. A wild post-earnings range has no tight flag to buy against, so it is only a bare red to green.

reasons: the tight flag as a gate is held (D-131, D-132) (+2)

questions.q: Is this a Go Signal?
choices: No; a red to green in mid-air
Yes; it turned in the window
Yes; any dip under it counts
No; it is a pivot, not a signal
questions.answer: No; a red to green in mid-air
questions.why: No. A red to green in mid-air has no level under it, so no level was tested and there is nothing to defend. The card wants a dip into the 20-day line or a marked level before the turn. Here the session low sits well above every moving average and marked level, so being on time does not save it.
questions.lesson_line: No level tested, nothing to defend.

wrong.Yes; it turned in the window: On time, but the turn has to come at a level it can defend.
wrong.Yes; any dip under it counts: The dip has to test the 20-day line or a marked level.
wrong.No; it is a pivot, not a signal: A pivot is a turn after the second candle. This one came on the second candle.

questions.story: The first candle dips under the prior close and the next closes above it. The session low sits well above every moving average and marked level.
questions.simple: No, because the turn tested no level, so there is nothing to defend.

deeper.trap: The trap is that the turn looks perfect on the clock. It dipped under the prior close and reclaimed it by the second candle. But the card wants the dip to come at a level, the 20-day line or a marked level. A turn with the session low far above every moving average has no level under it. A stop under that low defends nothing.

reasons: the level as a gate is held (D-130) (+2)

questions.q: Is this a Go Signal?
choices: Yes; candle two is in time
No; it needed the first candle
No; it is a pivot, not a signal
Yes; wait for a third to confirm
questions.answer: Yes; candle two is in time
questions.why: Yes. The reclaim comes by the end of the second hourly candle, and here candle two closed green back above the prior close. So it counts. The first candle does not have to reclaim. VIAV was this second-candle version and reached 44.2R, but one trade proves nothing about the next.
questions.lesson_line: First or second candle both count.

wrong.No; it needed the first candle: The first or the second candle counts. VIAV reclaimed on the second.
wrong.No; it is a pivot, not a signal: A pivot is a turn after the second candle. This one was on it.
wrong.Yes; wait for a third to confirm: Waiting past candle two turns it into a pivot. The close back above already came on the second.

questions.story: Candle one is red and stays under the prior close. Candle two closes green back above it. Everything else passes.
questions.simple: Yes, because the close back above the prior close came on candle two, which is still inside the window.

deeper.counter: A first-candle reclaim is not required. The card counts a turn in the first or the second candle. The second-candle version asks that candle one stays under the prior close and candle two closes green back above it. If the close back above comes on the third candle, it is a pivot, as AXON showed.

reasons: rests on the owner's criteria card (settled, D-145) (+2)

questions.q: What is this pattern?
choices: An Oops
A Go Signal
A U&R
A pivot
questions.why: An Oops. On our card an Oops gaps below the prior day's low and closes back above it on the daily bar. The Go Signal's line is the prior day's close, read on the first two hourly candles. Williams' Oops and Deepvue's Oops Reversal also use the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Daily bar and prior low: an Oops.

wrong.A Go Signal: The Go Signal line is the prior close, read on the first two hourly candles. This is one daily bar at yesterday's low.
wrong.A U&R: A U&R needs a prominent prior swing low and gives it up to 3 sessions on the daily chart. This story is just yesterday's low.
wrong.A pivot: A pivot is a turn later in the day, bought over the pivot candle's high. This story is one daily bar at yesterday's low.

questions.story: On the daily chart, a stock gaps under yesterday's low and closes back above yesterday's low by the end of the day.
questions.simple: It is an Oops, because it gaps under yesterday's low and closes back above it on the daily bar.

deeper.counter: The Go Signal's line is the prior CLOSE and the Oops line is the prior LOW. A stock can open under yesterday's close and still be above yesterday's low. That is no Oops.

reasons: card wording differs from outside sources (+1)

questions.q: Which of the card's context checks does it fail?
choices: The 20-day EMA trend
The 50-day SMA line
The 200-day SMA
The reclaim window
questions.why: The 20-day EMA trend. The card wants the 20-day EMA higher than it was 5 sessions ago. Here it is lower, so that check fails. Being above the 50-day and 200-day is not enough.
questions.lesson_line: Context first: the 20-day EMA should be rising.

wrong.The 50-day SMA line: The story has it above its 50-day, so that check passes.
wrong.The 200-day SMA: The story has it above its 200-day, so that check passes.
wrong.The reclaim window: A first-hour reclaim is inside the two-candle window.

questions.story: A first-hour reclaim in a stock above its 50-day and 200-day. Its 20-day EMA was 52.10 five sessions ago and is 51.40 today.
questions.simple: The 20-day EMA check fails, because the card wants it higher than it was 5 sessions ago and here it is lower.

deeper.trap: A tidy chart can still fail. This stock is above its 50-day and 200-day and the turn is on time, but its 20-day EMA is lower than it was 5 sessions ago. One check fails, so we pass.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (+2)

questions.q: Can you tell?
choices: No; you need the hourly bars
Yes; the wick shows the dip
Yes; green is red to green
No; wait for the next close
questions.answer: No; you need the hourly bars
questions.why: No. The daily footprint cannot show the turn, so grading from the daily chart is a listed mistake. A long lower wick could form at any hour, and a green close says nothing about the first two hourly candles. Open the hourly bars: the Go Signal lives in the first two hourly candles.
questions.lesson_line: Daily wicks hide the clock. Use hourly bars.

wrong.Yes; the wick shows the dip: A wick could be made any time of day. The Go Signal lives in the first two hourly candles.
wrong.Yes; green is red to green: A green daily close says nothing about the first two hours.
wrong.No; wait for the next close: Tomorrow tells you nothing about the first two hours of today. The hourly bars show them.

questions.story: You look at a daily chart. A candle has a long lower wick and a green close. A friend calls it a Go Signal.
questions.simple: No, because a daily candle hides the clock, so you must open the hourly bars to see the first two candles.

deeper.trap: A daily candle is one summary of the whole day. The same long-wick green candle can come from a first-hour reclaim, a midday recovery or a late push. Only the hourly bars show whether the stock traded under the prior close. They also show whether it got back above it by the end of the second hourly candle.

reasons: rests on the owner's criteria card (settled, D-145) (+2)

questions.q: Go Signal or pivot?
choices: A pivot over the candle high
A Go Signal, and a strong one
An Oops at the prior low
A U&R of a swing low
questions.answer: A pivot over the candle high
questions.why: A pivot. A turn later in the day, however clean, is a 30-minute pivot bought over the pivot candle's high. The Go Signal's reclaim must come by the end of the second hourly candle, and 13:30 is long past that. It is not an Oops or a U&R either: those are daily-bar patterns.
questions.lesson_line: Clean but late is a pivot.

wrong.A Go Signal, and a strong one: Too late in the day for a Go Signal, however clean the candle.
wrong.An Oops at the prior low: An Oops gaps below the prior day's low and closes back above it on the daily bar. This is an hourly turn against the prior close.
wrong.A U&R of a swing low: A U&R undercuts a prominent swing low and must close back above it within 3 sessions on the daily chart.

questions.story: The stock reclaims the prior close at 13:30 on a clean green candle at the 20-day line.
questions.simple: A pivot, because a turn later in the day is a pivot however clean it looks, not a Go Signal.

deeper.trap: Clean is not the same as in time. A candle at the 20-day line can look perfect. But the Go Signal is defined by the clock: the reclaim by the end of the second hourly candle. A later turn can still be traded as a 30-minute pivot, bought over the pivot candle's high. It is a different setup.

reasons: hourly bar alignment is held (D-031); 13:30 is late under either clock (+2)

questions.q: What does this trade teach?
choices: A big first candle widens the risk
A big first candle is a better signal
Never trade after 10:00
Always sell at the close
questions.answer: A big first candle widens the risk
questions.why: A big first candle widens the risk. NVDA's reclaim was the high of the day, the session closed under the prior close, and the stop was hit.
questions.lesson_line: A giant first candle leaves nothing to buy against.

wrong.A big first candle is a better signal: This one was the high of the day, and it was stopped the same session.
wrong.Never trade after 10:00: The window is the first two candles. The lesson is about the size of the first candle.
wrong.Always sell at the close: Selling at that close did not improve the average. The stop is the exit.

questions.story: The first candle closes at 126.81, up 2.3% and 2.7% from the stop. It was the high of the day. The session closes under the prior close.

questions.q: How do you file this?
choices: A planned loss; the risk was set
A mistake; you should have sold sooner
A reason to widen the next stop
A sign the setup has stopped working
questions.answer: A planned loss; the risk was set
questions.why: A planned loss. After the entry, a trade below the session low, the stop, is the exit. TSLA's turn was real, but the third candle broke back under the prior close and the fourth fell through the stop. A reclaim that does not follow through gives it back within hours. The size was set from that stop in advance.
questions.lesson_line: The turn was real. The stock gave it back. The stop paid.

wrong.A mistake; you should have sold sooner: The card's exit is the stop under the session low. Selling earlier is not part of the plan.
wrong.A reason to widen the next stop: We set the next stop the same way: a few cents under the session low, with the size coming from it.
wrong.A sign the setup has stopped working: One stop-out does not change the setup. After a stop-out, we buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade.

questions.story: You bought at 361.86 after a green first candle. The third candle broke back under the prior close, and the fourth fell through your stop at 353.79.
questions.simple: It is a planned loss, because the stop is the exit and the stock gave the turn back within hours.

deeper.example: TSLA: bought at 361.86 on the first candle with the stop at 353.79, which is 2.23% away. It was stopped the same session at the 12:30 candle, best 0.23R.

questions.q: What is the read?
choices: A reclaim by a cent proves little
A perfect Go Signal
A pivot
An Oops
questions.answer: A reclaim by a cent proves little
questions.why: It proves little. CRWD reclaimed by one cent, the next candle fell straight through the stop, and the stock lost 6% in two sessions.
questions.lesson_line: A reclaim by a cent is not strength.

wrong.A perfect Go Signal: It meets the clock, but a one-cent reclaim has no strength behind it.
wrong.A pivot: It is in the first candle, so the window is met.
wrong.An Oops: An Oops is a daily bar at the prior low.

questions.story: A gap-down open reclaims the prior close, 64.03, by one cent at the close of the first candle. You are asked to buy at 64.04.

questions.q: On our card, which turn is the better grade cue?
choices: A; it is stronger and earlier
B; it waited for confirmation
Same cue; both are in time
Neither; both turns are pivots
questions.answer: A; it is stronger and earlier
questions.why: A. On our card, a strong green hourly candle back above the prior close in the first candle is an A plus cue. A weak turn only in the second candle is a B minus cue. Both are in time, so both are Go Signals. A cue is a hint, not a score: grading is discretionary and hard to define.
questions.lesson_line: A strong early turn is a better cue than a weak late one.

wrong.B; it waited for confirmation: A turn only in the second candle, and weak, is a B minus cue.
wrong.Same cue; both are in time: The cues differ: a strong first candle is an A plus cue, a weak second candle is a B minus cue.
wrong.Neither; both turns are pivots: Both are inside the two-candle window, so both are Go Signals.

questions.story: Two Go Signals, both in time. A: a strong green first-candle reclaim. B: a weak turn only in the second candle.
questions.simple: A shows the stronger cue, because it turned strongly in the first candle while B turned weakly in the second.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the second candle as a flaw. It is not: both turns are in time, so both are Go Signals. The difference shows only in the grade, and only as a cue. A strong first-candle turn is an A plus cue, and a weak turn only in the second is a B minus cue.

reasons: grade cues sit beside the rulebook's note that grading is discretionary, E50 (+2)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Sell a big part of it now
Hold it all, it is working
Add, momentum is strong
Move the stop below the 50-day
questions.answer: Sell a big part of it now
questions.why: Sell a big part now. On a climax run in your own long, sell a big part into it. How big is a judgment call. You do not add. The stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Sell a big part into a climax run.

wrong.Hold it all, it is working: On a climax run in your own long, sell a big part into it.
wrong.Add, momentum is strong: We buy full size at one price with one stop, so there is nothing to add. A climax is when to sell, not buy.
wrong.Move the stop below the 50-day: Our stop sits a few cents under the session low at entry and only moves up. The 50-day is not the stop.

questions.story: Three days after the buy, your stock is in a climax run. It has risen three days straight, gapped up twice, and shows its widest range and highest volume of the run.
questions.simple: Sell a big part now, because the card says to sell into a climax run in your own long.

deeper.trap: 'It is working' is the reason people hold everything. The card names a climax run in your own long as the moment to sell a big part, and how big is a judgment call.

questions.q: How do you read it?
choices: Thesis over; the stop decides
Nothing yet; ignore the 50-day
Add a little on the dip
Move the stop to the 50-day
questions.why: The pullback thesis is over, but the stop is still the exit. A close under the 20-day EMA is a warning; a close under the 50-day ends the pullback thesis. Ending the thesis is not a sell order: the stop is the exit, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the 50-day ends the thesis. The stop still decides.

wrong.Nothing yet; ignore the 50-day: A close under the 50-day ends the pullback thesis.
wrong.Add a little on the dip: Entry is full size at one price with one stop, so there is nothing to add to.
wrong.Move the stop to the 50-day: The stop stays where the plan put it. The 50-day sits above the price now, so a stop there would just sell the position.

questions.story: You hold a Go Signal. The stock closes under its 50-day, though your stop is not hit yet.
questions.simple: The pullback idea is over once it closes under the 50-day, but your stop is still the exit.

deeper.counter: Read the two lines apart. A close under the 20-day EMA is only a warning. A close under the 50-day ends the pullback thesis. Neither is an exit by itself: the stop is the exit, and it only moves up. So you do not add, and you do not move the stop to a line that sits above the price.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line, go.context_break, and the owner's stop rule A4 (+2)

questions.q: The turn itself is the edge, because it happens in most sessions.
questions.why: False. The turn happens in about a third of all liquid sessions, so it is common. The stock and the level are the edge.
questions.lesson_line: The turn is common. The stock and the level are the edge.

questions.q: Which one is the Go Signal?
choices: Chart A
Chart B
Chart C
None of them
questions.why: Chart A. It dips under the prior close and reclaims it by the second hourly candle. Its trend is intact and the market is Green. B turns at 13:30, after the window, so it is a pivot. C never trades under the prior close, so it is not a Go Signal.
questions.lesson_line: Dip, reclaim in time, trend and market in line.

wrong.Chart B: A turn at 13:30 comes after the second hourly candle. That is a pivot, not a Go Signal.
wrong.Chart C: A gap up that never trades under the prior close is not a Go Signal.
wrong.None of them: Chart A passes every check in the story.

questions.story: A: a leader above its 50-day and 200-day, rising 20-day EMA, in a tight flag at its 20-day line. It dips under the prior close, then closes back above it in the second hourly candle, in a Green market. B: the same, but the turn comes at 13:30. C: a gap up all morning that never trades under the prior close.
questions.simple: A is the only one that dips, reclaims in time and has the trend and market in line.

deeper.trap: B and C can look stronger than A. B fails the clock, because a turn at 13:30 is after the second candle. C fails the dip, because a gap up that never trades under the prior close is not a Go Signal.

reasons: rests on our card with proposed gates (+2)

questions.q: What is the new stop, and what do you do?
choices: The 23.85 low is the stop; hold
Out at once; a gap is a full loss
Move the stop back up to 24.48
Buy more at the 23.85 gap low
questions.answer: The 23.85 low is the stop; hold
questions.why: The 23.85 low is the new stop, and you hold. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. The ceiling is this: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here one R is 24.48 minus 24.01, and a stop at 23.85 risks less than 2R. So you hold.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: first 30-minute low, unless past 2R.

wrong.Out at once; a gap is a full loss: The rule hands the stop to the first 30-minute low, and out only if that is past 2R.
wrong.Move the stop back up to 24.48: 24.48 is above the gap, so it would sell at once. The gap rule uses the first 30-minute low.
wrong.Buy more at the 23.85 gap low: We do not add. It is full size at one price with one stop.

questions.story: You bought a first-candle reclaim at 24.48 with the stop at 24.01, so one R is the gap between them. The next morning gaps through the stop. The first 30-minute low is 23.85.
questions.simple: The first 30-minute low becomes the new stop, and since that loss is under 2R you hold.

deeper.example: The buy at 24.48 with the stop at 24.01 is a real BE trade. The gap and the 23.85 low are made up to show the rule. That stop risks less than the 2R ceiling, so the gap rule keeps the trade.

questions.q: The stock's average daily volume is 400,000 shares. What is the most you may own?
questions.why: 4,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. One percent of 400,000 is 4,000. The limit ties your size to what the stock trades. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of daily volume is the ceiling.
questions.simple: One percent of 400,000 shares is 4,000, so that is the most you may own.

questions.q: Which one is a pivot, not a Go Signal?
choices: A; the turn came after the second candle
B; the gap up
C; the falling 20-day EMA
All three
questions.answer: A; the turn came after the second candle
questions.why: A. A turn after the second hourly candle is a pivot, not a Go Signal. B has no dip under the prior close, and C fails the rising 20-day check.
questions.lesson_line: Late turn, pivot. No dip, no signal. Falling 20-day, pass.

wrong.B; the gap up: B never traded under the prior close, so there is no turn at all, not a pivot.
wrong.C; the falling 20-day EMA: C was in time, but the context check fails. That is a pass, not a pivot.
wrong.All three: Only A is a pivot. B has no dip and C fails the 20-day check.

questions.story: Three charts. A: the close back above the prior close comes on the third hourly candle. B: a gap up that never dips under the prior close. C: a reclaim in the first candle with the 20-day EMA falling.

questions.q: Which one helps a Go Signal instead of blocking it?
choices: A rising 20-day EMA line
A report in two days
A gap up, green all day
Close under the 200-day
questions.why: A rising 20-day EMA. That is a point in its favor: the card wants it higher than it was 5 sessions ago. The other three are passes. A report in two sessions falls inside the 3-session no-buy window. A gap up that stays green all morning never trades under the prior close, so it is not a Go Signal. A stock under its 200-day gets no long.
questions.lesson_line: A rising 20-day helps. The other three block the trade.

wrong.A report in two days: No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report.
wrong.A gap up, green all day: A gap up that never trades under the prior close is not a Go Signal.
wrong.Close under the 200-day: No longs below the 200-day simple moving average.

questions.simple: A rising 20-day EMA helps the trade, while the other three each rule it out.

deeper.trap: A rising 20-day EMA is a plus, but it is not a rescue. It cannot fix a stock under its 200-day. It cannot fix a buy inside the 3 sessions before a report, or a gap up that stays green and never dips under the prior close. Each of those three rules the trade out, whatever the average does.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B22 and B26 (+2)
a NOT question whose key rests on a proposed card line, go.ema20_rising (+2)

questions.q: Skip the buy if the stock is more than 10% above its 200-day average.
questions.why: False. The stretch test is against the 10-day average, not the 200-day. Skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average. The card says not more than 10% above the 10-day at the buy. The 200-day is a separate trend rule: no longs below it.
questions.lesson_line: Ten percent over the 10-day: skip.
questions.simple: False, because the stretch test is against the 10-day average, not the 200-day.

questions.q: A Go Signal is built in two half-size buys to average the price.
questions.why: False. A Go Signal goes in at full size at once, with one price and one stop. We do not add. The size comes from the stop: account times risk percent, divided by the distance from entry to stop, rounded down, then capped.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, no adding.
questions.simple: False, because we buy the full size at one price with one stop and we do not add.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, A5 (+2)

questions.q: Our card wants the reclaiming hourly candle to be green: a close above its own open.
questions.why: True. Our card asks for a green reclaim candle, one that closes above its own open. Green here is about the candle's own open. The red-to-green line is still the prior close. Volume is not a rule, only a plus for grading.
questions.lesson_line: Our card wants a green reclaim candle: it closes above its own open.
questions.simple: True, because our card wants the reclaim candle to close above its own open, which makes it green.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (+2)

questions.q: What should the reclaiming hourly candle look like on our card?
choices: Green, closing above its open
Red, closing under its own open
A doji, closing right at its open
Any color, if the volume is high
questions.why: Green, closing above its open. Our card wants the reclaim candle to close above its own open. Volume is not a rule. More volume on the reclaim than on the flag's first hours is only a plus when you grade.
questions.lesson_line: Our card wants the reclaim candle green: a close above its open.

wrong.Red, closing under its own open: A red candle ends the hour under its open. Our card wants the close above it.
wrong.A doji, closing right at its open: A doji shows no push. Our card wants the close above the open.
wrong.Any color, if the volume is high: Our card treats volume as a plus for grading, not a rule, and it asks for a green candle.

questions.simple: The reclaim candle should be green, closing above its own open, and volume is only a plus.

reasons: rests on proposed card lines, go.reclaim_candle_green and go.volume (+2)

questions.q: A stock trades 600,000 shares a day on average, at about 24 dollars. How many million dollars trade a day?
questions.why: 14.4 million. Dollars traded a day is shares times price, 600,000 times 24. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one has the price but not the dollar volume, so it fails.
questions.lesson_line: Dollar volume is shares times price. Under $20 million a day, pass.
questions.simple: Shares times price gives dollars traded, and 600,000 times 24 is 14.4 million, under the 20 million floor.

questions.q: Our floors pass a $9 stock that trades $30 million a day.
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Both floors must hold. A $9 stock fails the price floor, however much it trades. Dollar volume of $30 million does not buy back a failed price floor.
questions.lesson_line: Two floors: $10 a share and $20 million a day.
questions.simple: False, because both floors must hold and a $9 stock fails the $10 price floor.

questions.q: How do you hold that stop?
questions.story: You buy a Go Signal at 26.43. The session low so far is 25.69, so the stop belongs a few cents under it.
choices: A real stop order with the broker
A mental stop; you watch the screen
An alert that pings you under the low
A stop you place after the first trim
questions.answer: A real stop order with the broker
questions.why: A real stop order with the broker. Every position has one, not a stop kept in your head. The stop sits a few cents under the session low, 25.69 so far, and it only moves up. In our scan that stop was 25.66.
questions.lesson_line: Every position has a real stop order. Your head is not a broker.

wrong.A mental stop; you watch the screen: A stop kept in your head is a debate, not a stop order.
wrong.An alert that pings you under the low: An alert only tells you. A stop order with the broker acts.
wrong.A stop you place after the first trim: Every position has a real stop order. It does not wait for the first trim.

questions.simple: Keep a real stop order with the broker, because a stop kept in your head is not a stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, D41 (+2)

questions.q: The stop only moves up, never down or wider, apart from the gap rule.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit and it only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception. After a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop, unless the loss there is past 2R. Then you get out.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only goes up. A gap through it hands it to the first 30-minute low.
questions.simple: True, because the stop only moves up, never down or wider, except under the gap rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, A4 and B20 (+2)

questions.q: Bought at 24.48, stop 24.01. One R is the gap between them. At what price does our breakeven window open?
questions.why: 25.42. One R is the fill minus the stop, 24.48 minus 24.01. Two R is the fill plus two of those. The breakeven move runs from 2R to 5R, ideally. It is a window, not a trigger you must hit at once.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven starts at 2R and runs to 5R.
questions.simple: Breakeven starts at 2R, so add two times the gap between fill and stop to the fill, giving 25.42.

questions.q: Can the stop go to breakeven now?
questions.story: You bought a Go Signal at 26.43 with the stop at 25.66, so one R is the gap between them. It trades to 27.00 and holds, up less than 1R. You want the stop at your entry.
choices: Not yet; breakeven starts at 2R
No; a stop never moves once set
Yes; 1R is enough to move it up
Yes; trail it under the 10-day line
questions.why: Not yet. The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R, ideally. This trade is up less than 1R, so it is not near 2R. The test is R. The trail comes later, for the last third after the trims.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven is earned in R, from 2R on.

wrong.Yes; 1R is enough to move it up: Too soon, and it is not even at 1R. The rule starts at 2R.
wrong.No; a stop never moves once set: The stop can move. It only moves up, never down or wider. Breakeven comes from 2R.
wrong.Yes; trail it under the 10-day line: The trail is for the last third, after the trims at 3R and 5R. At this price it is far too early.

questions.simple: Not yet, because our breakeven window starts at 2R and this trade is still under 1R.

questions.q: Bought at 26.43, stop 25.66. One R is the gap between them. At what price does our plan take the second third?
questions.why: 30.28. One R is the fill minus the stop, 26.43 minus 25.66. Five R is the fill plus five of those. After the first third at 3R, another third comes off at 5R, then you trail the last third. The trims are adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 5R before the open. The second third comes off there.
questions.simple: The second third comes off at 5R, which is the fill plus five times the gap between fill and stop.

questions.q: What comes next?
questions.story: You sold the first third of a Go Signal at 3R. Now the stock trades through 5R.
choices: Sell a third more; trail the rest
Skip the trim and trail it all
Sell the last two thirds now
Move the stop to breakeven, then hold
questions.answer: Sell a third more; trail the rest
questions.why: Sell another third and trail the rest. After the first third at 3R, another third comes off at 5R, then you trail the last third. The plan is adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: 3R for the first third, 5R for the second, then trail.

wrong.Skip the trim and trail it all: The plan takes another third at 5R first, then trails the last third.
wrong.Sell the last two thirds now: The plan trails the last third. It does not sell everything at 5R.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven, then hold: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. At 5R the plan takes another third.

questions.simple: Sell another third at 5R and trail the last third, because that is the plan after the first third at 3R.

questions.q: What is the plan now?
questions.story: You planned a Go Signal buy on a reclaim of the prior close. By the end of the second hourly candle, there is still no hourly close back over it.
choices: Drop it; no Go Signal today
Keep waiting; any hour will do
Buy now; the dip is deep enough
Buy tomorrow's open to catch it
questions.answer: Drop it; no Go Signal today
questions.why: Drop it. With no hourly close back over the prior close by the end of the second hourly candle, there is no entry. A later turn is a pivot (setup 41), not a Go Signal, and a pivot is bought over the pivot candle's high.
questions.lesson_line: Miss the first two hourly candles and the Go Signal is gone. Treat a later turn as a pivot.

wrong.Buy now; the dip is deep enough: Depth is not the test. The close back over the prior close is, and it has not come.
wrong.Keep waiting; any hour will do: The reclaim has to come by the end of the second hourly candle. After that it is a pivot.
wrong.Buy tomorrow's open to catch it: Buying the open before the turn is the blind open buy that gets stopped at the low.

questions.simple: Drop it, because the two-candle window has passed and a later turn is a pivot, not a Go Signal.

reasons: rests on the owner's criteria card (settled, D-145) (+2)

questions.story: The prior close is 50.00. The first hourly candle opens at 50.40, dips to 49.70 and ends the hour at 50.20. Everything else on the card passes.
questions.q: On our card, is this a Go Signal buy?
choices: No; the candle closed under its open
Yes; it closed back over 50.00
Yes; it traded under, then back over
No; the dip went too far under 50.00
questions.answer: No; the candle closed under its open

wrong.Yes; it closed back over 50.00: Back over 50.00 meets the red-to-green line. Our card also wants the reclaim candle green, above its own 50.40 open.
wrong.Yes; it traded under, then back over: That is the pattern. But our card also wants the reclaim candle to close above its own open, and this one closed under it.
wrong.No; the dip went too far under 50.00: The dip under the prior close is part of the pattern. What fails here is the candle's close under its own open.

questions.why: No, not on our card. The candle ended at 50.20, back over the 50.00 prior close but under its own 50.40 open. That makes it a red candle. Our card wants the reclaim candle green: it closes above its own open. Red to green itself is still measured against the prior close.
questions.lesson_line: Two tests: back over the prior close, and green against its own open.
questions.simple: No, because our card wants the reclaim candle to close above its own open, and this one closed under it.

Two definitions carry the name. This unit follows the criteria card, which follows the owner's rulings (D-145: red to green against the prior day's close, the first hourly candle under it, the reclaim by the end of the second hourly candle). The UNITS-method SET.34 row, the Model Book card and the glossary describe a different pattern: a catalyst gap that digests into the 9 EMA, then one wide candle that engulfs the pullback and closes above the catalyst high. The card retires that pattern (D-014). Nothing about the catalyst gap, the 9 EMA digest or the engulfing candle appears in this unit. The row's 'the confirmation layer for EP and PEG entries' is also not taught.

Hourly bars: the examples sit on intraday bars and the walk-throughs say 'hourly bars'.
